stories.title: DOOMQL
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
DOOMQL is a Doom-like game where SQLite is the game engine — not just storage. Movement, collision, rendering logic all run as SQL queries. Built by Peter Gostev using GPT-4.5 (referred to in the source as GPT-5.6 Sol, likely o3/GPT-4.5 era tooling).

↳ THE REAL STORY
This is a proof-of-concept that pushes SQL into territory it was never designed for: stateful, frame-by-frame game loop execution. Every tick — player position, raycasting, collision detection — is computed via SQL statements against SQLite tables. It works because SQLite is an in-process library with near-zero query overhead, making the absurd latency math just barely acceptable for a low-framerate game. For developers, the interesting part isn't the game itself but the architecture: it demonstrates that any sufficiently expressive query language can encode arbitrary state machines if you're willing to abuse it hard enough.
stories.considerations: The real question this raises isn't 'can you do this' — clearly you can — but what it says about AI-assisted development. Gostev used a frontier model to write code that no sane developer would write by hand, in a paradigm that has essentially no prior art or Stack Overflow to lean on. That's the pattern worth tracking: LLMs making deliberately unreasonable architectural experiments cheap enough to actually attempt. The catch is that the output is also nearly unmaintainable by humans — you get a working curiosity, not a codebase anyone extends.

stories.title: Using uvx in GitHub Actions in a cache-friendly way
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Simon Willison documented a cache-friendly pattern for using `uvx` in GitHub Actions by setting a `UV_EXCLUDE_NEWER` environment variable pinned to a specific date — preventing uv from fetching newer package versions and making the dependency resolution deterministic enough for cache hits.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The core problem: `uvx` resolves packages at runtime, and without version pinning, GitHub Actions cache keys mismatch on every run that pulls a newer package version — effectively making the cache useless. Setting `UV_EXCLUDE_NEWER` to a fixed date freezes the resolution window, so the cache key stays stable across runs. For workflows that call `uvx` frequently (linting, formatting, one-off CLI tools), this can shave meaningful seconds off CI times without requiring a full lockfile or explicit version pinning in the workflow YAML.
stories.considerations: The catch is maintenance overhead by stealth. A date-pinned `UV_EXCLUDE_NEWER` means you're silently drifting away from security patches and bug fixes in those tools — and unlike a dependabot-managed lockfile, there's no automated nudge to update it. Teams that set this and forget it could be running outdated versions of tools like `ruff` or `mypy` for months without noticing. Worth pairing with a calendar reminder or a periodic CI job that bumps the date deliberately.

stories.title: Tibo's tweets on Codex and ChatGPT Work updates
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
No verifiable product announcement or technical detail can be extracted from this source. The raw excerpt references Codex, ChatGPT Work, and Claude Code but contains no concrete numbers, feature names, API changes, or release notes — only a vague allusion to "fact checking numbers."

↳ THE REAL STORY
Insufficient signal to report. A tweet thread teasing a comparison between Codex and Claude Code metrics is not a briefing item until the actual data surfaces. Nothing here changes a workflow, a pricing model, or an integration path.
stories.considerations:
↳ WORTH WATCHING
The framing — "fact checking numbers against the sound of silence of Claude Code reporting" — hints at a transparency gap in how Anthropic surfaces usage or performance data for Claude Code compared to OpenAI's Codex. If that's the real story, it's worth watching when someone publishes the actual benchmark or billing comparison. Until then, this is a placeholder, not a finding.

stories.title: datasette code-frequency chart on GitHub
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Simon Willison checked his own GitHub code-frequency chart for the Datasette repository to measure whether coding agents and Claude Opus 4.5-class models have visibly changed his commit output over time.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The chart itself is a proxy metric — lines added/deleted per week — not a rigorous productivity study. But it's one of the few concrete, personal data points from a prolific open-source developer trying to quantify what AI-assisted coding actually does to throughput on a real, long-running project. If the chart shows a spike, it's a signal worth taking seriously precisely because Datasette has years of baseline data to compare against.
stories.considerations:
↳ WORTH WATCHING
Code frequency is a noisy signal. A spike in lines changed could mean more features shipped, or it could mean more AI-generated boilerplate, more refactors, or tests being written for the first time. Without pairing the chart with issue closure rate or feature milestones, it's easy to mistake activity for progress. The more interesting follow-up question: is the complexity per commit going up or down?
